title: WireGuard flap on-call notes + temporary mitigations
content:
Summary:

On 2026-03-10 at ~08:42 UTC several on-prem Private customers reported transient connectivity to Redwood control-plane (heartbeat gaps) and an increase in 5xx from the control-plane agent proxies. Root symptom was intermittent WireGuard session flaps between customer gateways and the private VPC egress nodes; in some cases the gateway's firewall silently dropped encrypted packets causing the VPN peer to rekey repeatedly. Impact was customer control-plane telemetry delays, a handful of short-lived job failures for model pulls, and elevated error rate for metrics collection.

Why this doc exists:
- Capture immediate on-call investigation notes (what we tried, what worked)
- Record short-term temporary mitigations we applied during the incident
- Draft a runbook section for WireGuard-facing customer firewall issues for the private-deployments folder
- Track action items for a permanent fix

Observed impact:
- Control-plane heartbeat gaps reported in metrics: heartbeat.missed per-customer spiked from ~0 to 12+ in windows of 30s.
- Agent proxies (edge-proxy private) returned 502/504 for transient requests when metrics/healthcheck returning timeout.
- Some customers reported manual restarts of gateway appliances cleared the issue temporarily.

Initial timeline (UTC):
- 08:39 — Pager triggered: multi-customer heartbeat gap alert (threshold: >5 missed in 60s)
- 08:42 — First on-call join, Slack thread created (#inc-wireguard-flap). Linked in linked_artifacts.
- 08:45 — Confirmed spike in heartbeats in Prometheus: query `sum by(customer)(increase(controlplane_heartbeat_missed[1m]))` shows 16 for three customers in eu-west-1 region.
- 08:50 — Ran quick checks on our egress nodes: `wg show` showed sessions staying up but with rapid handshake counts increasing for affected peers.
- 08:54 — Customer-provided fw logs (customer A) show repeated 'DROP UDP' lines for destination port 51820 from our egress IP range.
- 08:58 — Applied temporary mitigation: open UDP 51820 in edge NAT ACL for the affected VPC in eu-west-1 (see mitigations below).
- 09:05 — Heartbeat gap alerts subsided for those customers; metrics returned to baseline over ~90s.
- 09:30 — Postmortem sketch started (this doc).

What we checked (investigation commands / notes):
- WireGuard status: `sudo wg show all` -> sessions up but `handshakes` field jumping every 10-30s.
- Kernel conntrack: `sudo conntrack -L | grep <peer_ip>` -> entries existed but with rapidly changing timestamps. Suspected conntrack timeouts + firewall state.
- iptables/nftables on customer gateways: customer fw logs show 'DROP udp dpt:51820' matching kernel counters. Customer rules had a default DROP for unknown UDP flows older than X.
- tcpdump samples (on our egress node): `sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host <peer_ip> and udp` -> saw spikes of retransmitted UDP encapsulated packets followed by no response from customer gateway.
- BGP/route checks: routes were stable, no flaps on route(s) to customer subnets.
- Control-plane agent logs: elevated reconnect attempts, but no internal exceptions beyond timeouts.

Temporary mitigations applied (during incident):
- 08:58 — Added a temporary allow rule to the relevant edge NAT ACL for UDP 51820 from our egress IP block to the customer peer IP range (duration: 30m auto-revert). Implemented via infra-configs PR pipeline (see linked PR).
- 09:01 — Requested customer ops to inspect and add a short conntrack / firewall rule to allow established UDP flows (guidance: set conntrack timeout for UDP to >= 60s or add explicit accept rule for WireGuard peer IPs). Some customers applied the accept rule and reported immediate improvement.
- 09:10 — Enabled a short-lived fallback: when peer handshake rate exceeded threshold (10 handshakes/min) our edge-proxy toggled to use TCP-based control-plane keepalive via TLS fallback (only for control-plane management traffic). This is a stop-gap to reduce sensitivity to UDP drops.

Root cause hypothesis (why this happened):
- Customer firewall appliances were aggressively dropping UDP flows that they saw as stateless, combined with conntrack timeout settings that were too low for the handshake pattern WireGuard produced under our retransmit behavior.
- In some cases, middleboxes reset or silently filtered rekey/handshake packets leading to the peer rekeying loop.
- Contributing factor: our egress NAT devices do source IP churn across a small pool; customers' firewall rules keyed to exact IPs or ephemeral conntrack entries and therefore treated the encrypted traffic as new flows.

Why this is different from normal packet loss:
- Normal packet loss causes increased latency; here we observed deterministic handshake rekeying loops and firewall logs showing targeted packet drops (DROP UDP to 51820).

What worked (lessons from mitigation):
- Explicit firewall accept for WireGuard peer IPs stopped the flaps immediately for customers who could add the rule.
- Increasing UDP conntrack timeout on gateway appliances to >= 60s prevented session resets under retransmit.
- Short-term TCP/TLS fallback for control-plane reduced customer impact while networking teams coordinated with customers.

Runbook draft section: WireGuard flap due to customer firewall/middlebox
- Purpose: Steps for on-call to diagnose and mitigate transient WireGuard session flaps when customer on-prem firewall/middleware drops UDP handshake packets.
- Preconditions: access to edge-egress nodes, Prometheus dashboards, ability to propose infra ACL changes, contact path to customer ops.

Step 1: Validate symptoms
  - Check Prometheus: `increase(controlplane_heartbeat_missed[1m])` and `rate(edge_wireguard_handshakes_total[1m])`
  - If handshake rate > 5/min for any peer AND heartbeat_missed > threshold, mark as "wireguard-flap-suspect"

Step 2: Collect immediate evidence
  - On affected egress node: `sudo wg show` (note handshakes, latest-handshake, tx/rx bytes)
  - Start tcpdump: `sudo tcpdump -n -i <iface> host <peer_ip> and udp port 51820 -w /tmp/wg-peer-<peer_ip>.pcap` (collect ~30s)
  - Ask customer for firewall logs covering the timeframe (they often have syslog exports). Look for 'DROP udp dpt=51820' or similar.

Step 3: Quick mitigations (order matters)
  - If customer can immediately add a firewall accept for our egress IPs to the peer IP range: request that (preferred).
  - If not possible, propose infra ACL temporary tweak (allow UDP 51820 from our egress pool to the peer range) with auto-revert after 30m. Use infra-cfg PR and link in incident notes.
  - If neither is possible and impact is severe, enable control-plane TCP fallback for that customer (manual toggle in console) and notify product/security.

Step 4: Post-incident cleanup
  - Revert any temporary infra ACL changes (unless customer has made a permanent change).
  - Archive tcpdumps and firewall logs to the incident ticket.
  - Add timeline to incident doc and tag related network/runbooks page.

Open questions we need to resolve:
- Should we publish recommended firewall rule snippet for customers in Private onboarding docs? (short-term answer: yes)
- Can we reduce handshake sensitivity in our WireGuard implementation (tweak retransmit window or backoff)? Which component owns that change? (eng-serving-runtime / applied-ml / infra?)
- Is source IP churn across egress NAT pool necessary, or can we stabilize per-customer egress IP to reduce middlebox state churn? (impact on capacity and NAT exhaustion)
- What security review is required before recommending customers open UDP 51820 to our egress pool?

Action items (owners + target dates):
- [Samira] Draft firewall snippet for Private onboarding docs and link to Confluence runbook (due 2026-03-12).
- [Marco Ruiz] Evaluate feasibility of per-customer sticky egress IP allocation; quick notes and cost estimate (due 2026-03-19).
- [Ethan Brooks] Open a small RFC for WireGuard handshake backoff tuning in the serving runtime and tag eng-serving-runtime (due 2026-03-17).
- [Jing Wei] Add a runbook checklist entry and automation to create a temporary infra ACL PR template (due 2026-03-15).
- [Customer Success] Follow up with affected customers to confirm permanent firewall config changes and capture their appliance model/version (owner TBA, due 2026-03-18).

Notes for postmortem proper (if we escalate to postmortem):
- Collect all tcpdumps, conntrack snapshots, and firewall logs into S3 bucket `s3://redwood-incident-archive/INC-2026-03-10-01/` (automation to be created).
- Correlate control-plane error traces with handshake spikes using trace_id where available.
- Evaluate long-term options: conservative recommendation to customers (accept UDP 51820 from our egress pool, higher UDP conntrack timeout), and platform options (sticky egress IPs, handshake backoff).

Appendix: useful commands/log snippets
- `sudo wg show all` -> look for `latest handshake` timestamps and `handshakes` counter
- `sudo conntrack -L | grep <peer_ip>`
- `sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host <peer_ip> and udp port 51820 -vv`
- PromQL examples:
  - `sum by(customer)(increase(controlplane_heartbeat_missed[1m]))`
  - `sum by(customer)(increase(edge_wireguard_handshakes_total[1m]))`

Slack reference: thread started in #inc-wireguard-flap at 08:42 UTC (SLACK:threads/C12345abcde).

Immediate next steps for on-call now:
- Finalize and post the temporary mitigation notes to the incident ticket (SRE-3247).
- Ensure the infra ACL temporary change is auto-reverting and captured in PR.
- Notify customers that a recommended firewall change will go in onboarding docs and provide the snippet.

End of note.

(Working draft — will update as we collect more logs and customer appliance details.)
